new_statements.quote: The orthograpy used here follows Indonesian orthographical conventions. Sounds not found in Indonesian are the pharyngeal fricative [ħ], written as x, and the uvular stop [q], written as <q>. Sar also has a regular glottal fricative [h], written as <h>, and a glottal stop [Ɂ] written as <’>. Vowels that are pronounced long, are written as double vowels. When a double consonant is written, this indicates that the syllable following the double consonants is stressed.
new_statements.citation: Sir, Amos & Marian Klamer. 2018. Bahasa Sar. In: Booklet, Workshop on Documenting Minority Languages in Nusa Tenggara Timur, Indonesia (Kupang, 7-13 May 2018), pp. 97-103. Kupang: Universitas Kristen Artha Wacana.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: verbatim at, printed p. 99 = PDF p. 103 (extracted text), section "Sar orthographical notes"; the whole seven-line paragraph matches the reported quote character for character, including the typo "orthograpy". TOC confirms "Bahasa Sar.. 97" and "Sar orthographical notes.. 99"; Glottolog reference 580699 (Sir & Klamer 2018, "Bahasa Sar", pp. 97-103, Glottolog's most extensive description wordlist/minimal) matches the citation. Text layer present, 130-page booklet, produced May 2018. On the identity of the variety: the chapter describes Sar of Sargang and Lalafang, "central hills of northern Pantar", Timor-Alor-Pantar family, one active speaker Henrik Lambolang/Lembolang b. 1947; Glott…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only published statement is an orthographic convention: a written geminate consonant flags stress on the syllable after it (yiffar = jiˈfar 'dog', damman = daˈman 'ash', tallis = taˈlis 'to swim', hittar/yittar = jiˈtar 'road'), which implies that stress placement is not recoverable from the segmental string and has to be marked word by word. No default position is stated. The same collectors' 577-form field-note wordlist in LexiRumah (stress transcribed on 560 forms) shows a weight-sensitive tendency: closed or long-vowel final syllables usually carry the stress (gaˈfat, maˈnaːf, geˈtoːf), open short final syllables usually do not (ʔaˈlogar, ˈʔinaː), with lexical exceptions (ˈtewar 'to walk', ˈʔewar 'to return', ˈbrakaʔ 'to bless'). A reviewer may prefer 'weight-sensitive' on the wordlist evidence; the quoted statement alone supports only 'marked lexically'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in the source; the wordlist has penult-stressed CVCVC words (ˈtewar, ˈʔewar) beside the dominant final-stressed CVCVC type (jiˈfar, daˈman).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: citation forms in a 97-item wordlist (and a 577-item field-note list), elicited from the last active speaker, Henrik Lembolang (b. 1947, Sargang; also written Lambolang / Hendrik Bolang), in Kupang, May 2018. No sentence-level prosody described.
new_statements.identity_note: Sar = the language of Sargang and Lalafang, central northern Pantar (Glottolog sarr1247, under the Teiwa-Sar node teiw1236 next to Teiwa teiw1235). All 2018 data come from one speaker, Henrik Lembolang (spelled Lambolang in the booklet, 'Hendrik/Endi Bolang' in Klamer 2018), who left Sargang for Nule in 1965; he died in 2019 and Sar is now extinct. Earlier 'Sar (Adiabang variety)' wordlists (Baird 2003, Robinson 2010) used in the Alor-Pantar volumes are filed in LexiRumah as 'Teiwa, Adiabang' (teiw1235-adiab), so pre-2018 'Sar' data may belong to a Teiwa variety.

sources.note: No prose statement, but primary stress is transcribed on 560 of 577 forms (e.g. gaˈfat 'leg', jiˈfar 'dog', maˈnaːf 'cloud', ʔaˈlogar 'blue', ˈtewar 'to walk'). My count over the polysyllabic single-word forms: closed or long final syllables are stressed in about 153 of 177 disyllables, open short final syllables mostly not (9 final vs 42 penult, several of the latter being diphthong monosyllables) - a weight-sensitive tendency with lexical exceptions. Lect comment: the object-prefix vowel /a/ 'is sometimes pronounced as an unstressed reduced mid vowel'.
